title: Rent and Service Charge Setting 2026/27
filename: Rent Setting Paper 2026-27 - Board 28 January 2026 FINAL
author: P016
summary: Board paper approving a 4.8% (CPI + 1%) rent increase from 6 April 2026, the formula rent and affordable rent approach, service charge principles and the affordability tests. Approved by the Board on 28 January 2026.

version_history.change: Updated with September 2025 CPI of 3.8%; affordability tests added
Executive team review; resident consultation feedback added
Approved by the Board on 28 January 2026 (minute B26/003)

blocks.p: This paper asks the Board to approve rents and service charges for 2026/27, to take effect from Monday 6 April 2026. It covers social rent, affordable rent, older persons' and supported housing, shared ownership, market rent and leasehold service charges.

numbered: Approve an increase of **4.8%** (CPI of 3.8% at September 2025 plus 1%) for social rent, affordable rent and older persons' and supported homes, in line with the Regulator of Social Housing's Rent Standard.
Approve that homes let below formula rent continue to move to formula rent on relet only (no convergence for existing tenants).
Approve market rents at Week Street Apartments increasing by **4.0%**, below local market growth, to protect retention.
Note that shared ownership rents increase in line with each lease (older leases RPI + 0.5%; leases from 2021 CPI + 1%), capped by the Board at 4.8% this year as in previous years.
Approve the service charge principles in section 6, including the eligible / ineligible split and the target of full cost recovery within three years at sheltered schemes.

blocks.p: The Rent Standard allows registered providers to increase social and affordable rents by up to CPI + 1% each year. The government has confirmed CPI + 1% for ten years from April 2026, giving greater certainty for the business plan. September 2025 CPI was 3.8%, so the maximum permitted increase is 4.8%.

We manage {{fact:homes_total}} homes. The increase applies to {{sql:SELECT COUNT(*) FROM properties WHERE tenure IN ('Social rent','Affordable rent','Older persons & supported')|int}} rented homes. The current average weekly social rent is {{sql:SELECT AVG(weekly_rent) FROM properties WHERE tenure='Social rent'|gbp2}} and the average affordable rent is {{sql:SELECT AVG(weekly_rent) FROM properties WHERE tenure='Affordable rent'|gbp2}}.

The business plan approved in 2025 assumed CPI + 1% in 2026/27. Setting a lower increase would cost about £64,000 of income a year for every 0.1 percentage point below 4.8%, compounding over the 30-year plan. With interest cover headroom already tight (V2), the Executive Team does not recommend a lower increase.

Formula rent is calculated from the national average rent, relative county earnings, the property's January 1999 value and the number of bedrooms, adjusted by the rent caps. New social rent lets are set at formula rent, or formula rent plus 5% for new-build homes as the Rent Standard allows. Orchard Fields social rent homes are let at formula rent plus 5%.

Affordable rents are set at no more than 80% of the local market rent, **including service charges**, and capped at the Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rate for the Broad Rental Market Area so that rents remain covered by housing benefit and the housing element of Universal Credit. Market rents are re-valued at each new let and at every re-let.

table.caption: Table 1 - Affordable rents against market rent and LHA (illustrative, from the November 2025 valuation)

blocks.callout: From April 2026, 1-bed and 2-bed affordable rents will exceed the frozen LHA rate by between £3 and £6 a week. Around 70 households could face a shortfall if they rely on housing costs support. Income Recovery will contact these households before April and offer a Discretionary Housing Payment referral.
blocks.title: LHA risk

blocks.p: We test affordability in three ways each year:

bullets: **Living rent:** rents should not exceed 28% of lower-quartile earnings in the borough for a one-bed home. Social rents pass at all sizes; affordable rents fail for 3- and 4-bed homes.

**Residual income:** after rent and service charges, a household on Universal Credit should keep at least the government's 'minimum income' standard. The tightest case is a single person under 35 in a 1-bed affordable rent flat.
**Arrears trend:** current tenant arrears are {{fact:arrears_pct}} ({{fact:arrears_total}}), with {{fact:arrears_uc_share}} of arrears owed by Universal Credit households.

blocks.p: Residents on the Resident Scrutiny Panel were consulted on 9 January 2026. They accepted that the increase is needed to fund damp and mould works, but asked that letters explain the increase in plain English, show the new weekly and monthly amounts, and signpost the hardship fund.

Service charges recover the cost of services to a block or estate, such as communal cleaning, grounds maintenance, communal lighting and electricity, lift maintenance, door entry, fire safety equipment and, in SilverLiving schemes, the scheme coordinator and Careline. Service charges are set on actual cost, not on the CPI + 1% formula.

bullets: Charges are **variable** and based on the estimated cost for the year, with an annual reconciliation to actual cost within six months of the year end.
Each charge is split into **eligible** (covered by housing benefit / UC housing element) and **ineligible** (paid by the resident) elements.
Increases above 10% in a single year are phased over two years unless the Board agrees otherwise.
Management fee: 10% of service costs for tenants; 15% for leaseholders and shared owners to reflect section 20 and reconciliation work.
Leaseholders receive estimates by 28 February and the year-end account by 30 September, in line with their lease and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

blocks.p: The rent increase generates about £640,000 of additional rental income in 2026/27 compared with 2025/26 rents. Service charge income is estimated at £1.2m, an increase of 6.1%, driven by grounds maintenance and lift contract costs.

bullets: Higher arrears as rents rise during Universal Credit migration - mitigated by the hardship fund and earlier contact.
Reputational risk while TSM satisfaction is low - mitigated by clear letters that link the increase to investment.
LHA shortfall for affordable rent households - mitigated by targeted contact and DHP referrals.

blocks.p: The Board approved all five recommendations on 28 January 2026 (minute B26/003). Rent increase letters were posted on 27 February 2026, giving more than the required one month's notice.

title: Service Charge Policy
author: P016
summary: How Silvering sets, consults on, collects and reconciles service charges for tenants, leaseholders and shared owners, including section 20 consultation and disputes. Note: review date has passed.

version_history.change: Building safety costs and Building Safety Act leaseholder protections

blocks.p: This policy applies to every Silvering Homes resident who pays a service charge: tenants (social, affordable, older persons' and market rent), leaseholders (including right to buy) and shared owners. It does not cover rent, which is set under the Rent Setting framework.

bullets: We only charge for services we actually provide and that the tenancy agreement or lease allows.
Charges are reasonable, transparent and reflect the actual cost of the service.
We consult residents before introducing a new service or changing an existing one significantly.
We publish a breakdown of every charge and how it was calculated.

numbered: Finance prepares estimates in January using contract prices and the previous year's actual costs.
Each cost is apportioned across homes by the method in the lease or tenancy (usually equal shares per home, or by bedroom size where the lease says so).
A management fee is added (10% tenants; 15% leaseholders and shared owners).
Estimates are sent to leaseholders and shared owners by 28 February and to tenants with the rent increase letter.

blocks.p: We prepare actual cost accounts by 30 September each year. Where the actual cost is more than the estimate, the difference is added to the following year's charge (spread over 12 months on request). Where it is less, the surplus is credited to the resident's account. Differences of less than £10 per home are carried forward rather than invoiced.

Where qualifying works will cost any leaseholder more than £250 in a year, or a long-term agreement will cost any leaseholder more than £100 a year, we carry out statutory consultation under section 20 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985: a notice of intention, a 30-day observation period, a statement of estimates and a further 30-day observation period. Where we cannot consult, we must apply to the First-tier Tribunal for dispensation.

Under the Building Safety Act 2022, qualifying leaseholders in buildings of 11 metres or more are protected from the costs of remediating historical safety defects. At Rosemount Tower these costs are met by Silvering and are not recharged. Routine fire safety costs (for example fire alarm servicing) remain recoverable.

Where a lease allows, we collect a contribution to a reserve fund for future major works such as lift replacement. Reserve funds are held in a separate designated account and reported in the year-end account.

Residents can ask for a detailed breakdown and inspect invoices within six months of receiving the year-end account. If a query is not resolved, it is handled through the complaints procedure. Leaseholders may also apply to the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) to determine whether a charge is reasonable.
Leaseholders facing large major works bills can pay by interest-free instalments over up to 36 months (up to 10 years for bills above £10,000, subject to a charge on the property).

title: Procurement and Contract Management Policy
author: P038
summary: Procurement thresholds, purchase order rules, the no PO no pay principle, the Procurement Act 2023 requirements and how contracts are managed and recorded in the contracts register.

version_history.change: Aligned with Northway Finance Cloud purchase-to-pay workflow
Updated for the Procurement Act 2023 (in force 24 February 2025)

blocks.p: This policy makes sure Silvering Homes buys goods, works and services lawfully, gets value for money for residents and manages contracts so that suppliers deliver what we pay for.

rows: One written quote; purchase order raised
Budget holder and Head of Service
Formal quotation via Procurement; published on the central digital platform if above £30,000
£100,001 up to the Procurement Act threshold
Competitive tender or compliant framework call-off
Above the Procurement Act threshold (works £5.37m; services £214,904 for housing associations)
Procurement Act 2023 procedure or framework; notices published
table.caption: Table 1 - Procurement thresholds

blocks.h1: 3. Purchase orders: no PO, no pay

bullets: A purchase order (PO) must be raised in Northway Finance Cloud **before** goods, works or services are ordered.
Suppliers must quote the PO number on every invoice. Invoices without a valid PO number are returned to the supplier and are not paid.
Responsive repairs subcontractors must also quote the FieldLoop job number for each line, so we can match cost to a property and check the work was done.
Retrospective POs are only allowed in an emergency and must be approved by the Financial Controller within two working days.

blocks.p: Every contract over £25,000 has a named contract manager and is recorded on the contracts register, with start and end dates, extension options and a performance RAG rating reviewed quarterly. Procurement must start at least nine months before a contract over £100,000 expires. A contract must not continue past its end date on an informal extension: any extension must be allowed by the contract and confirmed in writing by the Director.

Anyone involved in a procurement must declare any interest using the declaration form before evaluation starts. Board members' interests are recorded in the register of interests held by the Head of Governance.
Tenders above £100,000 include at least 10% of the quality score for social value, such as local jobs, apprenticeships for residents and support for community projects.

title: Value for Money Statement 2025/26
author: P002
summary: Silvering's published value for money statement for 2025/26: the regulator's seven VFM metrics against targets and peers, our own efficiency measures and the 2026/27 targets.

blocks.p: The Regulator of Social Housing's Value for Money Standard requires us to make the best use of our resources to deliver our objectives and to publish evidence of how we do this. This statement forms part of our 2025/26 financial statements and was approved by the Board on 22 July 2026.

2025/26 was a year of heavy investment in existing homes. We spent more than ever on damp and mould and building safety, brought in a second damp and mould surveyor, and prepared for Awaab's Law. That investment shows in a higher cost per home and lower operating margin, which we planned for and explained to the regulator.

rows: Headline social housing cost per unit
table.caption: Table 1 - Regulator's VFM metrics. Peer group: eight mid-sized Kent and South East housing associations.

bullets: Overall tenant satisfaction (TSM TP01, 2025/26): {{fact:tsm_overall_2526}}.
Average relet time: {{fact:void_days_avg_12m}} days in the last 12 months (target 28).
Current tenant arrears: {{fact:arrears_pct}}.
Gas safety compliance: {{fact:gas_compliance}}.
Bringing repairs in-house continues to save an estimated £310,000 a year against the old contract, despite subcontractor costs from vacancies.
Re-tendering grounds maintenance (Greenway Grounds) saved £14,000 a year - but resident complaints show quality must be monitored.
Moving to Northway Finance Cloud removed £22,000 of legacy licence and server costs.
Cost per unit is above peers because of damp and mould and building safety. We expect it to stay high for two more years.
New supply was low because Orchard Fields phase 1 completed in October 2026, after the year end.
Subcontractor spend to cover trades vacancies is poor value. Filling electrician posts is the single biggest repairs efficiency lever.

numbered: Fill trades vacancies and cut subcontractor spend by 30%.
Hit Awaab's Law timescales without increasing cost per case.
Let the remaining Orchard Fields phase 1 homes quickly to cut void loss.
Use Microsoft 365 Copilot to save administrative time in finance, repairs and customer services, measured through the pilot.

title: Treasury Management Report - Quarter 2 2026/27
filename: Treasury Management Report Q2 2026-27 - ARC 19 Nov 2026
author: P002
summary: Draft Q2 treasury report for the Audit & Risk Committee: debt and facilities, liquidity, covenant compliance and forecast, hedging and treasury policy compliance at 30 September 2026.

blocks.p: At 30 September 2026 Silvering Homes was compliant with all loan covenants and with the Treasury Management Policy. Liquidity is sufficient for 21 months of committed spend against a policy minimum of 18 months. The forecast EBITDA-MRI interest cover for 2026/27 has fallen from 118% (budget) to **114%**, driven by higher repairs subcontractor costs and the damp and mould programme. This is still above the 110% covenant but below the Board's golden rule of 115%.

Total drawn debt is £56.7m, of which 84% is at fixed rates (policy range 60% to 90%). Undrawn facilities total £7.3m. The revolving credit facility was drawn by £1.5m in September to fund Orchard Fields phase 2 payments to Castlemere Construction.

blocks.callout: Forecast interest cover of 114% breaches the Board's 115% golden rule (not a lender covenant). The Executive Team will consider mitigations at the budget kick-off on 17 November, including deferring £250,000 of planned works and the timing of phase 3.
blocks.title: Golden rule

blocks.p: Cash at bank was £4.1m. The 18-month cash flow forecast includes Orchard Fields phase 2 payments of £6.8m and phase 2 Homes England grant receipts of £1.5m at start on site and practical completion.
Surplus cash is held with two banks rated A or above and in a money market fund, within the policy limit of £3m per counterparty.
The Committee is asked to note the report and the forecast golden rule breach, and to ask the Executive Team to bring mitigation options to the December Board.

subject: October month-end - accruals and invoices needed by Friday
summary: Ian Mackie chases budget holders for October accruals and coding; the Brightline September invoice without a PO or job numbers is still on hold, and Daniel Kerr explains why.

messages.body:
Morning all,

October month-end closes on Friday 6 November. Please can you send me, by 12 noon Wednesday 4 November:

1. Accruals for any work done in October that hasn't been invoiced yet (supplier, amount, PO number, cost centre).
2. Confirmation that you've approved all invoices sitting in your Northway approval queue. There are currently 23 invoices over 10 days old waiting for approval.
3. Any big one-off costs coming in November that we should know about for the forecast.

Daniel - Brightline invoice BEL-26-0937 for September is still on hold. It has no PO number and none of the lines have FieldLoop job numbers, so Ben can't match it. It also includes 30 EICRs, which is a lot more than usual. Can you or Rob confirm what we're paying for? Under the procurement policy it's no PO, no pay, and I can't accrue it at Month 6 without knowing it's valid.

Sophie has the Month 6 variance commentary in draft and still needs words from Priti (planned works) and Daniel (damp and mould, subcontractors). Please reply to her directly.

Thanks,
Ian

Ian,

The work is genuine. Brightline picked up a batch of overdue EICRs at Brenchley Gardens and Coxheath Lane in September because we've got no electricians to spare - Rob asked them to do it to stop the backlog getting worse. Somebody should have raised a PO and I'll take that one on the chin.

Rob will send Ben the list of addresses from Assure360 today so the EICR line can be matched. The repairs lines are from FieldLoop - Kwame can pull the job numbers.

Planned works and damp words to Sophie by Wednesday, promise.

Dan

Hi both,

I've had the EICR schedule from Rob - 30 addresses, all match Assure360. I've asked Brightline to reissue the invoice with PO-4500-1187 and the job references, as they did for June to August. They've said this is the third time this year an invoice has gone out without them.

Can I suggest we raise a blanket PO for the EICR catch-up work through to March? It would stop this happening every month. It's still within their contract value, but we're on track to spend more than the £142k annual value if usage stays like this.

Ben

Thanks Ben. Agree to a blanket PO up to the contract value - please raise it and send it to Daniel to approve.

I'm copying Martin because the subcontractor overspend is already about £95k adverse at Month 6, and the Brightline trend needs to go into the budget kick-off on the 17th.

Ian
